title: "Audit Analytics in Excel"

::: {.learning-objectives}
## Learning Objectives {.unnumbered}

After completing this chapter, you will be able to:

1. Explain how internal and external auditors use data analytics on whole populations, and reconcile a population to the general ledger before testing it.
2. Stratify a population by value and use the strata to direct audit attention.
3. Perform a first-digit test of Benford's Law, measure conformity with the mean absolute deviation, and explain a nonconformity that has a legitimate cause.
4. Age receivables at an as-of date, reconcile the aged detail to the general ledger, and select balances for confirmation.
5. Test journal entries for characteristics of management override, combine the results into a risk score, and record a disposition for each exception.
6. Design duplicate, gap, and threshold tests, and document audit analytics in a workpaper that another auditor can review.
:::


::: {.chapter-slides data-chapter="chapter-08"}
:::

## Opening Scenario {.unnumbered}

Charles River's audit committee has asked the internal audit team for a data-driven review before the external auditors begin their work on fiscal 2026. You have joined the team, and the chief audit executive has given you three areas to review: the supplier payments of fiscal 2024 through 2026, the accounts receivable at the end of fiscal 2026, and the journal entries of the same three years.

The earlier chapters followed a staff accountant through the question of the Furniture margin. Along the way, they turned up conditions that an auditor would want to examine, from the reused supplier invoice numbers of Exercise 2.6 to the invoices dated before their orders in Exercise 5.2. This chapter takes the auditor's view. Its question is not what the numbers mean for the business but whether they can be relied on: whether each population is complete, whether any transactions look unusual, and whether the ledger agrees with the detail behind it.



## Audit Analytics and the Internal Auditor

Internal auditors work for the organization they audit. They evaluate its risk management, controls, and governance, and they report to the audit committee of the board of directors. External auditors are independent of the organization and express an opinion on its financial statements. The two roles differ in purpose, but they rely on much of the same evidence, and increasingly on the same analytics: both need to know whether recorded transactions are complete and valid, and whether the controls over them operated as designed.

Traditional audit procedures examine a sample of transactions and draw conclusions about the rest. Data analytics lets an auditor examine every record in a population instead: every payment, every invoice, every journal entry. The American Institute of Certified Public Accountants (AICPA) publishes a *Guide to Audit Data Analytics* that addresses how auditors can use such analyses, including practical considerations for assessing the reliability of the data they use (AICPA, 2026).

Testing a whole population changes the nature of the work. A test that examines tens of thousands of records returns a list of exceptions, the records that meet its criteria, and most exceptions turn out to have an ordinary explanation. The auditor's judgment goes into designing the test, investigating each exception, and deciding what it means. @fig-08-01 shows the workflow that this chapter follows.

![An Audit Analytics Workflow.](/visuals/svg/fig-08-01-audit-analytics-workflow.svg){#fig-08-01 fig-alt="A diagram of six steps in a row, joined by arrows: the objective, which states the risk the test addresses and what an exception would look like; the population, which is imported and agreed to the ledger; the tests, which stratify, profile, and flag records; the exceptions, which are examined against source documents; the disposition, which classifies each exception as expected with evidence, to follow up, or a misstatement; and the workpaper, which records the work for a reviewer. A dashed arrow loops back from the exceptions to the tests, labeled to refine the test and rerun it when most exceptions are false positives."}

The earlier chapters have already covered two parts of an audit. Chapter 3 described the auditor's requirement to understand a client's information system and how its data flows to the ledger (AICPA, 2021), and the analytical procedures in the exercises of Chapters 6 and 7 compared recorded amounts with an expectation, as the auditing standard of the Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (PCAOB) describes (PCAOB, n.d.-b). This chapter turns to tests of individual transactions: which payments, invoices, and entries deserve a closer look, and why.

::: {.callout-warning .watch-out icon=false}
## Watch out
Charles River's year-end closing entries, dated December 31, move each year's revenue and expenses to retained earnings. Any analysis of revenue or expenses by period must leave them out, as Chapter 7 did when it compared operating expenses with the budget. A journal entry test must do the opposite and include them: a closing entry is a journal entry like any other, and entries at the end of a period are the ones that auditing standards single out for attention.
:::


## Reconciling the Population

A population is the complete set of records to which a test's conclusion applies, such as every supplier payment dated in the period under review. Before you test a population, confirm that you have all of it. A test on an incomplete extract may find nothing wrong simply because the problem records were never extracted. The check is the control total you have used since Chapter 4: agree the count and total of the extract to an independent source.

For transactions that post to the ledger, the general ledger is that source. Every Charles River supplier payment credits the cash account, so the count and total of the payments in an extract should equal the count and total of the cash credits that payments posted in the same period. Fay and Negangard (2017) begin their journal entry testing case with the same step, validating that a file of entries is complete before testing it.

Defining the population also means defining its period. Charles River's ledger already holds a few hundred supplier payments dated early in fiscal 2027, for invoices of fiscal 2026. A review of fiscal 2024 through 2026 filters them out by payment date, and the ledger comparison uses the same cutoff, so that both sides describe the same population.


## Stratification

Stratification divides a population into groups, or strata, usually by value. A stratification table reports the number of items and their total value in each stratum, and the share of the population that each represents. It answers a simple question that shapes the rest of the audit: where are the dollars? A population of payments typically contains many small items and a few large ones, and the few large ones can carry a large share of the value.

Auditing standards use stratification in two ways. For audit sampling, the PCAOB's standard on sampling notes that separating a population into relatively homogeneous groups, based for example on the recorded value of the items, can reduce the sample size the auditor needs. A sample always carries sampling risk, the risk that the conclusion drawn from the sample differs from the one the whole population would support. The same standard therefore directs the auditor to examine in full the items for which accepting any sampling risk is not justified. Examples are items that could individually equal or exceed tolerable misstatement, the largest misstatement in an account that, combined with misstatements elsewhere, would not make the financial statements materially misstated (PCAOB, n.d.-d). Such items are often called individually significant items. In analytics, where every item is tested anyway, a stratification table still directs attention: the largest items are examined one by one, and the strata that hold most of the value receive the most careful tests.

In Excel, the strata are defined by lower and upper bounds typed in cells, and COUNTIFS and SUMIFS with a pair of criteria, greater than or equal to the lower bound and less than the upper bound, count and total each stratum. Keeping the bounds in cells makes them parameters: you can change a bound and see the table recalculate, and a reviewer can see exactly where each boundary lies.


## Benford's Law

### The Expected Pattern of First Digits

In many collections of numbers, the first digit is far more often a 1 than a 9. Newcomb (1881) noticed that the early pages of books of logarithm tables, which cover numbers that begin with 1, wore out faster than the later ones, and Benford (1938) tested the pattern on many different kinds of data. Benford's Law gives the expected proportion of numbers whose first digit is d as `LOG10(1+1/d)`: about 30 percent start with 1, about 18 percent with 2, and fewer than 5 percent with 9. The pattern arises in data that are produced by multiplying and combining many quantities, span several orders of magnitude, and have no built-in minimum or maximum, which describes many accounting amounts.

Nigrini and Mittermaier (1997) introduced digit tests based on the law as analytical procedures that auditors could use in planning: because authentic numbers tend to follow the expected frequencies, a population whose digits depart from them may contain invented or altered amounts, and deserves attention.

Not every population should conform, and Nigrini (2017) reviews which kinds of audit data are appropriate for a Benford analysis, a question the analyst must answer before running the test. Numbers that are assigned rather than measured, such as invoice numbers or check numbers, carry no information about magnitude. Amounts constrained by a minimum or a maximum, or a subset of a population selected by its size, cannot spread across the digits as the law expects. And amounts that are set by people, such as prices ending in 99, follow the preferences of the people who set them.

### Measuring Conformity

A first-digit test counts how many amounts begin with each digit from 1 to 9 and compares each digit's actual proportion with its expected proportion. The comparison needs a summary measure, and the usual statistical tests are of little help with accounting data. A chi-square test compares all nine counts with their expected values at once, and a z test compares one digit at a time. With tens of thousands of amounts, both find a statistically significant difference in almost any population, however small the difference. Nigrini (2012) recommends instead the mean absolute deviation (MAD), the average of the nine absolute differences between the actual and expected proportions, and gives the ranges in @tbl-08-01 for judging the first-digit test.

| MAD of the first-digit test | Conclusion |
|---|---|
| 0.000 to 0.006 | Close conformity |
| 0.006 to 0.012 | Acceptable conformity |
| 0.012 to 0.015 | Marginally acceptable conformity |
| Above 0.015 | Nonconformity |

: First-digit conformity ranges for the mean absolute deviation {#tbl-08-01}

### From a Pattern to Transactions

A nonconforming first-digit test does not show that anything is wrong. It shows where to look. The digits with the largest differences, and the subsets of the population that produce them, lead to the transactions that need an explanation, and the explanation is often a feature of the business: a pricing policy, a fee schedule, or a way of paying invoices. Nigrini (2017) examined a proposed method that selects as an audit sample the transactions whose removal would make a population conform, and found that it can produce large samples of questionable accuracy. Benford analysis is best used as it is used in Tutorial 8.1, to point the auditor toward subsets that deserve a closer look.

## Aging and Reconciling Receivables

### The Aging Schedule

An aging schedule classifies the unpaid invoices at an as-of date by how long they are past their due date, in buckets such as current, 1 to 30 days, 31 to 60 days, 61 to 90 days, and over 90 days. It serves the credit department, which follows up the oldest balances, and it serves the accountants who estimate how much of the receivables will not be collected.

Under U.S. generally accepted accounting principles, the standard of the Financial Accounting Standards Board (FASB) on credit losses requires an allowance for credit losses: a valuation account, deducted from the receivables, for the amount not expected to be collected. The standard lists methods based on an aging schedule among the acceptable ways to estimate it, and it requires the estimate to reflect the risk of loss even when that risk is remote. It illustrates the method with historical loss rates for each age bucket, adjusted for current conditions and reasonable and supportable forecasts (FASB, 2016). Charles River's chart of accounts calls this account 1030 Allowance for Doubtful Accounts, the older name for the same valuation account.

Aging depends on dates, so it depends on the as-of date described in Chapter 5. An invoice's balance at the as-of date is its total minus the payments and credits recorded on or before that date. Payments applied after the as-of date must be excluded, or the aging will show the receivables as they are today rather than as they were at the reporting date.

### Reconciling the Detail to the Ledger

The open invoices are the detail behind the accounts receivable account in the general ledger, a sub-ledger in the terms of Chapter 2. At any date, the two should agree. A reconciliation lists the balance of the ledger account, the total of the detail, and every reconciling item that explains a difference between them. Some reconciling items are expected, such as a receipt recorded in the ledger before it was matched to its invoices, and each one should clear in a later period. An item that cannot be explained is a finding in itself: either the ledger holds an amount that no invoice supports, or the detail is missing invoices that the ledger recorded. Either way, the aging does not describe the whole balance, and an allowance estimated from it would not cover the whole balance either.

### Confirming Balances and Selecting a Sample

A reconciliation shows that the detail and the ledger agree, but both are records kept by the company. External evidence comes from the customers themselves. A confirmation asks a customer to state the balance it owes directly to the auditor. The PCAOB's standard on confirmation requires the auditor to confirm accounts receivable that arise from sales of goods or services, or otherwise to obtain the evidence directly from a knowledgeable external source. In selecting the receivables to confirm, the auditor takes into account the nature of the items that make up the balances (PCAOB, n.d.-c).

Confirming every balance is rarely practical, so the auditor selects. The largest balances are confirmed in full as individually significant items, and the rest are sampled. The sampling standard requires a sample to be selected so that it can be expected to represent the population, which means that every item must have an opportunity to be selected. Random-based selection achieves this, whether it draws from the population as a whole or from each stratum separately, a method called stratified random sampling (PCAOB, n.d.-d).

In Excel, `RANDARRAY(n)` returns n random numbers between 0 and 1, and `SORTBY(array, by_array)` sorts one array by the values of another. Sorting a list of customers by a column of random numbers therefore shuffles it, and the first rows of the shuffled list are a random sample. RANDARRAY draws new numbers every time the workbook recalculates, however, so the selection must be frozen with Paste Values as soon as it is made, and its date and parameters recorded. A selection that cannot be reproduced cannot be reviewed.

## Journal Entry Testing

### Management Override

Every control depends on the people who operate it, and the people at the top of an organization are in a position to override it. Management override of controls, the ability of managers to bypass controls that work for everyone else, is a risk in every organization, and journal entries are one of the main ways it can be carried out. Auditing standards therefore treat journal entries as a focus of every audit.

The PCAOB's standard on fraud, AS 2401, observes that material misstatements due to fraud often involve recording inappropriate or unauthorized journal entries during the year or at the end of a period. It requires the auditor to identify and test journal entries for evidence of such misstatement, and it describes characteristics that fraudulent entries often have, among them:

- entries made to unusual or seldom-used accounts;
- entries made by individuals who typically do not make journal entries;
- entries recorded at the end of a period, or as post-closing entries after the period's books have been closed, with little or no explanation;
- entries that contain round numbers or a consistent ending number.

The standard adds that the testing should ordinarily focus on the end of the period, while considering whether entries throughout the period also need testing (PCAOB, n.d.-e).

@tbl-08-03 translates these characteristics, and three further indicators used in practice, into tests on Charles River's JournalEntry table. The table records who created each entry and when, who approved it and when, the date it posts to, its type, and its total. The Employee table adds each approver's approval limit, MaxApprovalAmount. Fay and Negangard (2017) build their journal entry case around the same kinds of questions: who recorded an entry, when it was created, how it was described, and whether it was posted to an earlier date than the one on which it was made.

| Characteristic | Charles River columns | Test in Tutorial 8.3 |
|---|---|---|
| Made by individuals who typically do not make journal entries (AS 2401) | CreatedByEmployeeID | Entries by creator |
| Recorded at the end of a period or after it (AS 2401) | PostingDate, CreatedDate | Backdated flag |
| Round numbers or a consistent ending number (AS 2401) | TotalAmount | RoundAmount flag |
| Created at an unusual time | CreatedDate | Weekend flag |
| Approved by the person who made it | CreatedByEmployeeID, ApprovedByEmployeeID | SelfApproved flag |
| Approved above the approver's authority | TotalAmount, MaxApprovalAmount | AboveLimit flag |

: Characteristics of journal entries and the tests that look for them {#tbl-08-03}

Two of the tests need a word of explanation. A backdated entry is one created on a later day than the date it posts to, so that it changes a period that may already have been reported; it is the journal entry counterpart of a post-closing entry. An entry approved by the person who created it defeats segregation of duties, the principle that no one person should both initiate and approve a transaction.

Digit tests can be applied to journal entries too, but with care. When Debreceny and Gray (2010) examined the journal entries of 29 organizations, the first digits of the amounts departed from Benford's Law in every one of them, so a nonconforming digit test on journal entries is not unusual and does not by itself suggest fraud. Characteristics of the kind in @tbl-08-03 are more direct: each one identifies specific entries and a specific question to ask about them.

### Risk Scores and Dispositions

Each flag in @tbl-08-03 is a TRUE or FALSE value, and adding the flags gives a risk score: the number of characteristics an entry has. A risk score is a way to rank entries for review, not a probability of fraud. An entry with one flag often has an ordinary explanation, while an entry with several flags combines characteristics that are individually common but rarely occur together without a reason. The weights are a judgment, too. Adding the flags treats them as equally important, and an auditor may decide that some matter more.

Most flagged entries are false positives: entries that meet a test's criteria but are legitimate. Nigrini (2019) classified the numbers used in fraud schemes by their patterns, such as round amounts, amounts just above or below control thresholds, and duplicates of authentic transactions. Nigrini emphasizes that the analysis should include refining and rerunning the tests, and grouping and filtering the results, to deal with false positives. The auditor records a disposition for every exception: expected, with the evidence that explains it; follow up, with the question to ask and the document to request; or a misstatement or a control deficiency, a weakness in the design or operation of a control that keeps it from preventing or detecting misstatements on time, to be reported. A test whose exceptions are mostly expected is refined, for example by excluding a recurring type of entry that has been examined once, and rerun, as the dashed loop in @fig-08-01 shows.


{{< include _tutorial-03.qmd >}}


## Duplicate, Gap, and Threshold Tests

### Duplicates and Near-Duplicates

Exercise 2.6 tested for exact duplicates: supplier invoice numbers and check numbers that appear twice for the same supplier. A duplicate payment does not always repeat a reference number, so auditors also look for near-duplicates: records that agree on the fields that matter but differ in one, such as the same supplier and amount on different dates. In Excel, COUNTIFS can flag every payment whose supplier and amount appear more than once, and adding the invoice as a third criterion separates a second payment of the same invoice from two invoices of the same amount.

At Charles River, about a hundred pairs of payments share a supplier and an amount on different dates, about a dozen of them within thirty days of each other, and every pair pays two different invoices. Each pair is therefore a false positive with evidence: two invoices of the same amount, each paid once. The test is still worth running, because a near-duplicate that pays the same invoice twice is exactly the error that an exact-duplicate test misses. Exercise 8.5 asks you to run it.

### Gap Tests

Documents numbered by a system should form a continuous sequence, and a gap may mean a document that was deleted or never recorded. A quick test for each numbering series compares the number of documents with the range of their numbers: if the largest number minus the smallest, plus one, exceeds the count, numbers are missing. Charles River's sales invoice, journal entry, purchase order, and cash receipt numbers run without gaps within each year, a clean result that the workpaper should record as carefully as an exception.

A gap test also needs a series that is meant to be continuous. Charles River's check numbers follow the numbering of all its supplier payments, so the payments made by ACH or wire transfer leave thousands of gaps in the check sequence. Matched against the payment numbers, every gap is explained by a payment of another kind, except the numbers of the two checks that reused an earlier check number, the pairs you met in Exercise 2.6.

### Threshold Tests

People who want to avoid a control often keep amounts just below the threshold that would trigger it, and amounts just above or below control thresholds are one of the patterns Nigrini (2019) found in fraud schemes. A threshold test counts the items in narrow bands just below and just above each threshold, such as the approval limits in the Employee table's MaxApprovalAmount column, and looks for a concentration below the line. The same test extends to consecutive documents with the same requester and amount, which may be one purchase split to stay under a limit. Exercise 8.5 applies it to Charles River's purchase requisitions.

### Tests from Earlier Chapters

Several tests from earlier chapters belong in the same audit program, the planned set of procedures for an engagement. Exercise 2.5 found purchase requisitions converted to orders without an approver. Exercise 5.2 tested invoice numbers against invoice dates and found invoices whose number carries a different year from their date, and invoices dated before their orders. Exercise 5.5 matched supplier addresses against employee addresses, and Exercise 5.6 reviewed the supplier and item master files for suppliers that were never approved and items sold outside their active life. Each is a test of a control, and each belongs in the workpapers with its population, its results, and a disposition for every exception.

::: {.callout-tip .in-practice icon=false}
## In Practice
Pricing is a control area where approval records and transactions can tell different stories. A promotion's approval sets the dates when its discount may be used, and a price override request must be approved before an order is billed at the lower price. A price list, too, is valid only between its effective dates. Testing these controls means comparing the transactions with the approvals: the order dates of promotion lines with the promotion's effective dates, the order dates of price-list lines with the list's effective dates, and the prices billed with the status of the override requests. Exercise 8.6 carries out these tests on Charles River's sales.
:::


## Documenting Audit Analytics

An audit test is only as useful as its documentation. The PCAOB's standard on audit documentation requires enough information for an experienced auditor with no previous connection to the engagement to understand the work performed, the evidence obtained, and the conclusions reached, and to identify who performed and who reviewed the work (PCAOB, n.d.-a). The documentation worksheet you built in Chapter 4 recorded the purpose, sources, parameters, and open questions of an analysis. An audit workpaper, like the one in @fig-08-09, adds what an auditor needs to rely on the analysis: the objective of the test, the reconciliation of the population to the ledger, the exceptions and their dispositions, and a conclusion.

Analytics adds two requirements of its own. The first is reproducibility. A workbook whose queries import the data and whose formulas perform the tests can be refreshed and rerun, but only if the workpaper records which extract it used, its as-of date, and the parameters of each test, such as the strata bounds, the aging buckets, and the approval limits. The second is the treatment of exceptions. A test that flags dozens of records is not complete until each one has a disposition and the evidence behind it, and a test that flags nothing is a result to be recorded, not a reason to omit the test.

::: {.callout-note .connecting-dots icon=false}
## Connecting the Dots
The tests in this chapter rest on the skills of the earlier chapters: importing and filtering Tables with Power Query, merging tables on their keys, conditional aggregation, and PivotTables. They also reach the limits of a workbook. A test that compares every payment with every other payment, or every journal entry line with every account, becomes slow in a worksheet long before it becomes difficult in a database. The later Parts of the book return to the same tests with SQL, which can join and compare whole tables in a single query, and with interactive reports that let a reviewer move from a summary of exceptions to the transactions behind it.
:::


## Looking Ahead

This chapter has looked at the Charles River data as an auditor does. You reconciled populations to the ledger before testing them, stratified the supplier payments to see where the dollars are, and used a first-digit test to find a group of payments whose digits depart from Benford's Law for a reason that the payment process explains. You aged the receivables at the end of fiscal 2026, found that the ledger holds a balance that no invoice supports, and selected customer balances for confirmation. You tested every journal entry for characteristics of management override, ranked them with a risk score, and traced the highest-scoring entry to the same balance. Along the way, you recorded a disposition for every exception and documented each test in a workpaper.

This chapter completes Part II. The [Part II Comprehensive Case](#sec-case-part-2) that follows brings the techniques of all five Excel chapters together on a decision: whether Charles River should run its calendar of promotions again in 2027. Part III then turns from the workbook to the database, where the same questions can be asked of whole tables at once.
